claim: The method detects single apoferritin molecules in vitreous ice with high specificity.
source: Our method detects single apoferritin molecules in vitreous ice with high specificity and determines their orientation and location precisely.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental results showing detection of apoferritin in cryo-EM images with high SNR values and correct orientation determination.

claim: The method determines the orientation and location of apoferritin molecules precisely.
source: Our method detects single apoferritin molecules in vitreous ice with high specificity and determines their orientation and location precisely.
evidence: Experimental data shows angular differences within detected orientations were less than three degrees from the best-detected orientation.

claim: High spatial-frequency information is essential for optimal detection.
source: Simulations show that high spatial-frequency information and—in the presence of protein background—a whitening filter are essential for optimal detection, in particular for images taken far from focus.
evidence: Simulations demonstrate that SNR increases with inclusion of higher spatial frequencies.

claim: A whitening filter is essential for optimal detection in the presence of protein background.
source: Simulations show that high spatial-frequency information and—in the presence of protein background—a whitening filter are essential for optimal detection, in particular for images taken far from focus.
evidence: Simulations show that whitening restored detectability in images with protein background.

claim: Small viral RNA polymerase molecules can be detected inside rotavirus particles.
source: Experimentally, we could detect small viral RNA polymerase molecules, distributed randomly among binding locations, inside rotavirus particles.
evidence: Experimental detection of VP1 polymerase in rotavirus DLPs using constrained searches.

claim: The detection threshold is 150 kDa in ice based on currently attainable image quality.
source: Based on the currently attainable image quality, we estimate a threshold for detection that is 150 kDa in ice and 300 kDa in 100 nm thick samples of dense biological material.
evidence: Experimental data showing detection of apoferritin fragments down to 150 kDa with SNR above detection threshold.

claim: The detection threshold is 300 kDa in 100 nm thick samples of dense biological material.
source: Based on the currently attainable image quality, we estimate a threshold for detection that is 150 kDa in ice and 300 kDa in 100 nm thick samples of dense biological material.
evidence: Simulations with protein background showing approximately 30% reduction in SNR, leading to doubled molecular weight threshold.

claim: Atomic-resolution snapshots of cells are impossible due to radiation damage.
source: Much could be inferred from atomic-resolution snapshots of cells, although this is known to be impossible due to radiation damage (Breedlove and Trammell, 1970; Henderson, 1995; Glaeser, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on radiation damage in electron microscopy.

claim: Detection of unlabeled proteins in cells on the basis of template matching is possible.
source: What is possible, however, is the detection of unlabeled proteins in cells on the basis of template matching.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental detection of proteins in rotavirus particles and apoferritin in ice.

claim: Template matching in tomograms has made it possible to map the 3D locations and orientations of individual ribosomes in thin regions of unstained frozen-hydrated cells.
source: This approach has made it possible to map the 3D locations and orientations of individual ribosomes (Ortiz et al., 2006; Pfeffer et al., 2015) and proteasomes (Asano et al., 2015) in thin regions of unstained frozen-hydrated cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work demonstrating ribosome detection.

claim: Template matching in tomograms has made it possible to map the 3D locations and orientations of individual proteasomes in thin regions of unstained frozen-hydrated cells.
source: This approach has made it possible to map the 3D locations and orientations of individual ribosomes (Ortiz et al., 2006; Pfeffer et al., 2015) and proteasomes (Asano et al., 2015) in thin regions of unstained frozen-hydrated cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work demonstrating proteasome detection.

claim: The optical resolution of a tomogram is approximately 4 nm.
source: The optical resolution of a tomogram (~4 nm; Oikonomou and Jensen, 2016) allows the 3D locations of individual structures, once detected, to be determined accurately.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on tomogram resolution.

claim: Detectability in tomograms is limited to structures large enough to be distinct in shape at approximately 4 nm resolution.
source: Detectability is limited, however, to structures large enough to be distinct in shape at this resolution; in practice, only a few protein complexes in the megadalton range have been detected reliably using information in tomograms alone (but see Beck et al., 2009; Kühner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and the stated resolution limit of tomograms.

claim: Only a few protein complexes in the megadalton range have been detected reliably using information in tomograms alone.
source: Detectability is limited, however, to structures large enough to be distinct in shape at this resolution; in practice, only a few protein complexes in the megadalton range have been detected reliably using information in tomograms alone (but see Beck et al., 2009; Kühner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on template matching in tomograms.

claim: Template matching in tomograms is difficult in crowded regions of cells because nearby macromolecules can obscure the protein-of-interest's outline.
source: Template matching in tomograms is difficult in crowded regions of cells because nearby macromolecules can obscure the protein-of-interest's outline and thus interfere with detection (Frangakis et al., 2002; Grünewald et al., 2003; Beck et al., 2009; Asano et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on challenges in template matching.

claim: Use of a protein's fine internal structure for template matching should allow more robust detection but also requires higher resolution.
source: Use of a protein's fine internal structure for template matching should allow more robust detection, but also requires higher resolution.
evidence: Logical inference based on the need for high-resolution information to distinguish fine structural details.

claim: At sufficiently high spatial resolution, the projected 2D potential of a protein is unique for a particular protein and projection direction.
source: The approach is based on the fact that–at a sufficiently high spatial resolution–the projected (2D) potential of a protein, and thus the pattern of phase shifts imparted on the electron wave as it passes through the sample, is unique for a particular protein and projection direction.
evidence: Based on fundamental principles of electron scattering and protein structure uniqueness.

claim: Projection-matching concepts have been used in single-particle analysis to select particle images.
source: Projection-matching concepts have been used in single-particle analysis (SPA) to select (Penczek et al., 1992; Huang and Penczek, 2004) and align (Grigorieff, 2007) particle images, although low-resolution templates are preferred in order to limit bias in any resulting reconstructions (Henderson, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on single-particle analysis methods.

claim: Projection-matching concepts have been used in single-particle analysis to align particle images.
source: Projection-matching concepts have been used in single-particle analysis (SPA) to select (Penczek et al., 1992; Huang and Penczek, 2004) and align (Grigorieff, 2007) particle images, although low-resolution templates are preferred in order to limit bias in any resulting reconstructions (Henderson, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on single-particle analysis methods.

claim: Low-resolution templates are preferred in single-particle analysis to limit bias in reconstructions.
source: Projection-matching concepts have been used in single-particle analysis (SPA) to select (Penczek et al., 1992; Huang and Penczek, 2004) and align (Grigorieff, 2007) particle images, although low-resolution templates are preferred in order to limit bias in any resulting reconstructions (Henderson, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henderson 2013 on template bias.

claim: The unambiguous detection of single proteins using existing high-resolution structural information is not affected by template bias.
source: Different from the SPA case, which aims to determine new high-resolution structures, we are here concerned with using existing high-resolution structural information for the unambiguous detection of single proteins, which is not affected by template bias.
evidence: Logical distinction between structure determination (affected by bias) and detection (not affected by bias).

claim: Effects of macromolecular background are greatly reduced by using close-to-focus images.
source: We find that effects of macromolecular background are greatly reduced by using close-to-focus images and matched filtering, both of which suppress low-frequency information.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations and experiments showing improved detection at close-to-focus settings.

claim: Effects of macromolecular background are greatly reduced by using matched filtering.
source: We find that effects of macromolecular background are greatly reduced by using close-to-focus images and matched filtering, both of which suppress low-frequency information.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations showing whitening filter restores detectability.

claim: Proteins can be reliably detected down to a size limit of 150 kDa in vitreous ice.
source: We show experimentally that we can reliably detect proteins down to a size limit of 150 kDa in vitreous ice.
evidence: Experimental data showing detection of apoferritin fragments at 150 kDa.

claim: The detection limit should increase to 300 kDa in a 100 nm thick tissue slice based on simulations that include macromolecular background.
source: Simulations that include a macromolecular background suggest that this limit should increase to 300 kDa in a 100 nm thick tissue slice.
evidence: Simulations with BSA background showing reduced SNR leading to higher molecular weight threshold.

claim: Better detectability might be achieved using higher-resolution reference structures.
source: Even better detectability might be achieved using higher-resolution reference structures.
evidence: Simulations showing improved SNR when using lower B-factors (higher resolution structures).

claim: Experiments involving viral proteins in intact rotavirus particles demonstrate detectability in the presence of protein and nucleic acid background.
source: Experiments involving viral proteins in intact rotavirus particles demonstrate detectability in the presence of protein and nucleic acid background.
evidence: Experimental detection of VP1 and ASU in rotavirus DLPs.

claim: The expectation value for the electron count in each pixel can be calculated directly from the known three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in the target and the optical parameters of the electron microscope.
source: The expectation value for the electron count in each pixel can be calculated directly from the known three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in the target and the optical parameters of the electron microscope (Rullgard et al., 2011; Vulović et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to methods for calculating electron scattering from atomic models.

claim: Cross-correlation allows a match to be detected even when multiple proteins overlap in projection as long as the image-intensity modulation is approximately equal to the sum of the individual proteins' contributions.
source: Cross-correlation allows a match to be detected even when multiple proteins overlap in projection as long as the image-intensity modulation is approximately equal to the sum of the individual proteins' contributions, as is the case for weak-phase objects (e.g. ref. Reimer and Kohl, 2008, p. 316).
evidence: Supported by citation to textbook on weak-phase object approximation.

claim: Cross-correlation is able to extract matching information even if individual pixels are dominated by noise as long as the spatial resolution of the microscope is preserved.
source: Cross-correlation is able to extract matching information even if individual pixels are dominated by noise as long as the spatial resolution of the microscope as such is preserved, which is the case when using motion-corrected electron movies (Brilot et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to motion correction methods and fundamental signal processing principles.

claim: Searching a single cryo-EM image for a target protein with a high-resolution reference structure requires cross-correlating millions of templates.
source: Searching a single cryo-EM image for a target protein with a high-resolution reference structure requires cross-correlating millions of templates (see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), each corresponding to a different orientation of the target with an image (typically megapixel-sized), or in other words, searching a space of location-orientation combinations (LOCs) with more than 1012 entries.
evidence: Calculation based on the number of orientations and image pixels.

claim: The computational cost of a search goes up linearly with the number of templates.
source: Since the computational cost of a search goes up linearly with the number of templates, we chose a set of orientations spaced as evenly as possible, thereby minimizing, for a given number of orientations, the largest rotation that is necessary to bring any orientation into alignment with a member of the set.
evidence: Based on computational complexity of cross-correlation operations.

claim: A set of approximately 2.4 × 10^6 orientations generated using the Hopf fibration method has an incremental rotation angle between one set member and its closest neighbor of 1.88 degrees.
source: In a set of ≈2.4 × 106 orientations generated in this way, the incremental rotation angle between one set member and its closest neighbor was 1.88 degrees.
evidence: Calculated from the Hopf fibration orientation set.

claim: Out of 10,000 random orientations, none required a rotation of more than 1.51 degrees to bring it into alignment with one of the members of the Hopf set.
source: Out of 10,000 random orientations, none required a rotation of more than 1.51 degrees to bring it into alignment with one of the members of the Hopf set (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Computational validation of the Hopf orientation set coverage.

claim: Correlation-based projection-matching can correctly identify proteins and determine their locations and orientations in simulated images.
source: After confirming in simulated images that correlation-based projection-matching can correctly identify proteins and determine their locations and orientations (data not shown), we tested whether this could also be done in experimental images.
evidence: Stated as confirmed through simulations, though data not shown.

claim: For images taken close to focus, there were typically only a small number of orientations for which the corresponding cross-correlograms contained pixels with exceptionally high SNR values.
source: For images taken close to focus, where the target molecules are not detectable by eye (Figure 1a), there were typically only a small number of orientations for which the corresponding cross-correlograms (CCGs) contained any (and when they did, only a few) pixels with values of the SNR (the ratio of the peak height and the standard deviation of the CCG noise [Saxton and Frank, 1976], Materials and methods) that were exceptionally high, i.e., substantially exceeded those expected for a Gaussian noise distribution (Figure 1b).
evidence: Experimental observation from apoferritin images.

claim: High-value CCG pixels were typically clustered at locations that in high-underfocus images were encircled by the dark ring typical for apoferritin.
source: High-value CCG pixels were typically clustered at locations that—in high-underfocus images—were encircled by the dark ring typical for apoferritin (Figure 1d).
evidence: Experimental observation correlating detection locations with visible apoferritin features.

claim: The angular differences within the set of orientations associated with a cluster of high-valued CCG pixels were less than three degrees away from the best-detected orientation after taking into account the octahedral symmetry of apoferritin.
source: The angular differences within the set of orientations associated with a cluster of high-valued CCG pixels were less than three degrees away from the best-detected orientation after taking into account the octahedral symmetry of apoferritin (97.9% of values both >7.32 and within one pixel of any peak, N = 17 peaks).
evidence: Statistical analysis of detected orientations in experimental images.

claim: The search procedure is highly specific to a particular protein structure.
source: The sharp dependence of the CCG value on orientation suggested that our search procedure is highly specific to a particular protein structure.
evidence: Inferred from the sharp orientation dependence of CCG values.

claim: For GroEL (decoy protein), the amplitude distribution of CCG values lacked the high-amplitude tail seen for the target apoferritin.
source: For GroEL the amplitude distribution of CCG values lacked the high-amplitude tail seen for the target, and instead followed the distribution expected when cross-correlating a set of Gaussian-noise templates with an image also containing Gaussian white noise (Figure 1e).
evidence: Experimental comparison of target and decoy protein searches.

claim: Without radiation damage, the SNR should increase with the square root of the accumulated electron exposure.
source: Without radiation damage, the SNR should increase with the square root of the accumulated electron exposure because both the peak height and the noise variance increase linearly with the exposure.
evidence: Based on fundamental signal and noise scaling principles.

claim: The SNR initially increased at approximately the expected rate with an exponent of 0.508 ± 0.033.
source: In our experiments, we found that the SNR (averaged over the ten largest distinct peaks in one image) initially increased at approximately the expected rate (with an exponent of 0.508 ± 0.033), but levelled off at an exposure of around 1000 electrons per nm2 (Figure 2a).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR vs. exposure.

claim: The SNR levelled off at an exposure of around 1000 electrons per nm^2.
source: In our experiments, we found that the SNR (averaged over the ten largest distinct peaks in one image) initially increased at approximately the expected rate (with an exponent of 0.508 ± 0.033), but levelled off at an exposure of around 1000 electrons per nm2 (Figure 2a).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR vs. exposure showing saturation.

claim: The average SNR varied with molecular weight with an exponent of 0.508 ± 0.009 for experimental images.
source: Then, cross-correlating the fragment templates with the experimental images, we found that the average SNR varied with the MW as expected (Figure 2b, fitting y = a*(MW)α to the CCG values for the 5 × 24 fragments and the full template yielded α = 0.508 ± 0.009 and α = 0.514 ± 0.003 for experimental and simulated images, respectively; two particles).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR vs. molecular weight for apoferritin fragments.

claim: The average SNR varied with molecular weight with an exponent of 0.514 ± 0.003 for simulated images.
source: Then, cross-correlating the fragment templates with the experimental images, we found that the average SNR varied with the MW as expected (Figure 2b, fitting y = a*(MW)α to the CCG values for the 5 × 24 fragments and the full template yielded α = 0.508 ± 0.009 and α = 0.514 ± 0.003 for experimental and simulated images, respectively; two particles).
evidence: Simulated measurement of SNR vs. molecular weight for apoferritin fragments.

claim: Proteins down to approximately 150 kDa should be detectable when using an SNR of 7.32 as the detection threshold.
source: This suggested that we should be able to detect proteins down to a MW of roughly 150 kDa when using an SNR of 7.32 as the detection threshold, which should generate about one false alarm (CCG values above the threshold due to noise) per image of 18502 pixels (Materials and methods).
evidence: Inference from the molecular weight dependence of SNR and the chosen detection threshold.

claim: An SNR threshold of 7.32 should generate about one false alarm per image of 1850^2 pixels.
source: This suggested that we should be able to detect proteins down to a MW of roughly 150 kDa when using an SNR of 7.32 as the detection threshold, which should generate about one false alarm (CCG values above the threshold due to noise) per image of 18502 pixels (Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from Gaussian noise statistics.

claim: Full searches for 200, 150, and 100 kDa fragments yielded 259, 58, and 10 CCG values >7.32, respectively.
source: We found, respectively, 259, 58, and 10 CCG values >7.32, of which most (256, 56, and 8) were within 0.3 nm of locations where peaks had been detected using the full-protein templates (440 kDa; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental full search results for apoferritin fragments.

claim: A reduction in SNR by 20% was caused by a positional misalignment of 0.15 nm in experimental images.
source: We found (Figure 2c–e) that a reduction in the SNR by 20% was caused by a positional misalignment of 0.15 nm in experimental images (0.13 nm in simulations), a focus mismatch of 21.0 nm (15.5 nm), or a magnification error of 1.9% (1.6%).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR sensitivity to positional mismatch.

claim: A reduction in SNR by 20% was caused by a focus mismatch of 21.0 nm in experimental images.
source: We found (Figure 2c–e) that a reduction in the SNR by 20% was caused by a positional misalignment of 0.15 nm in experimental images (0.13 nm in simulations), a focus mismatch of 21.0 nm (15.5 nm), or a magnification error of 1.9% (1.6%).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR sensitivity to focus mismatch.

claim: A reduction in SNR by 20% was caused by a magnification error of 1.9% in experimental images.
source: We found (Figure 2c–e) that a reduction in the SNR by 20% was caused by a positional misalignment of 0.15 nm in experimental images (0.13 nm in simulations), a focus mismatch of 21.0 nm (15.5 nm), or a magnification error of 1.9% (1.6%).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR sensitivity to magnification error.

claim: For the axis perpendicular to the image plane (z-axis), a mismatch of 0.95 degrees was sufficient for a 20% drop in SNR.
source: While for the axis perpendicular to the image plane (z-axis) a mismatch of 0.95 degrees (0.89 in simulations) was sufficient for a 20% drop in SNR, for an axis parallel to the image plane 1.92 degrees (1.34) were needed (Figure 2f).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR sensitivity to orientation mismatch.

claim: For an axis parallel to the image plane, 1.92 degrees were needed for a 20% drop in SNR.
source: While for the axis perpendicular to the image plane (z-axis) a mismatch of 0.95 degrees (0.89 in simulations) was sufficient for a 20% drop in SNR, for an axis parallel to the image plane 1.92 degrees (1.34) were needed (Figure 2f).
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR sensitivity to orientation mismatch.

claim: The lower sensitivity for rotations around an in-plane axis is likely caused by the foreshortening of the atomic movements as their z-components are lost upon projection.
source: The lower sensitivity for rotations around an in-plane axis is likely caused by the foreshortening of the atomic movements as their z-components are lost upon projection.
evidence: Logical inference from projection geometry.

claim: At 2000 nm underfocus, the peaks in the CCG possess a sharply defined maximum with a peak SNR quite comparable to that seen for much smaller defocus values.
source: Using simulations, we also explored the effect of the focus setting on detection and found that at 2000 nm underfocus the peaks in the CCG flare out towards a broad base but still possess a sharply defined maximum (Figure 3a) with a peak SNR quite comparable to that seen for much smaller defocus values.
evidence: Simulation results showing CCG peak characteristics at different defocus values.

claim: For isolated target proteins, the detectability did not depend strongly on the defocus.
source: This means that, at least for isolated target proteins, the detectability did not depend strongly on the defocus.
evidence: Inference from simulation results showing similar SNR across defocus values for isolated proteins.

claim: Searching the 70 nm underfocus image with protein background yielded a clear peak at the correct location with SNR of 14.4 compared to 16.9 for the background-free case.
source: The apoferritin target could not be detected by eye in either image, yet searching the 70 nm image yielded a clear peak at the correct location albeit with reduced SNR compared to the background-free case (14.4 vs. 16.9).
evidence: Simulation results comparing detection with and without protein background.

claim: Template matching was not able to reliably detect the target in the 2000 nm underfocus image with protein background.
source: Template matching was, however, no longer able to reliably detect the target in the 2000 nm image (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Simulation results showing failed detection at large defocus with protein background.

claim: As the defocus becomes smaller, low spatial frequencies are increasingly suppressed.
source: As the defocus becomes smaller, low spatial frequencies are increasingly suppressed, the number of phase reversals is reduced, and the suppression of high spatial frequencies, which is caused by the fact that the illumination is only partially coherent, becomes much less severe (Figure 3b).
evidence: Based on the properties of the contrast transfer function at different defocus values.

claim: As the defocus becomes smaller, the number of phase reversals is reduced.
source: As the defocus becomes smaller, low spatial frequencies are increasingly suppressed, the number of phase reversals is reduced, and the suppression of high spatial frequencies, which is caused by the fact that the illumination is only partially coherent, becomes much less severe (Figure 3b).
evidence: Based on the properties of the contrast transfer function at different defocus values.

claim: As the defocus becomes smaller, the suppression of high spatial frequencies becomes much less severe.
source: As the defocus becomes smaller, low spatial frequencies are increasingly suppressed, the number of phase reversals is reduced, and the suppression of high spatial frequencies, which is caused by the fact that the illumination is only partially coherent, becomes much less severe (Figure 3b).
evidence: Based on the properties of the contrast transfer function and coherence envelope.

claim: In simulated PPM images, the target protein was neither visible by eye nor could it be detected by cross-correlation.
source: In simulated PPM images the target protein was neither visible by eye nor could it be detected by cross-correlation (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Simulation results for phase-plate microscope without whitening.

claim: The loss of detectability against protein background seen for simulated PPM and large-defocus images is caused by low-spatial-frequency noise.
source: This suggested that the loss of detectability against protein background seen for simulated PPM and large-defocus images is caused by low-spatial-frequency noise that happens to be suppressed by the close-to-focus CTF.
evidence: Inference from comparison of detectability across different imaging conditions.

claim: For simulations that included protein background, the image noise was dominated by low-frequency components both at 2000 nm defocus and for the PPM.
source: For simulations that included protein background, the image noise was dominated by low-frequency components, both at 2000 nm defocus and for the PPM (Figure 3c).
evidence: Analysis of power spectral density from simulated images.

claim: To optimize detection, one needs to use the full matched-filtering concept, which includes a whitening filter.
source: This suggested that to optimize detection one needs to use the full matched-filtering concept (McDonough et al., 1995), which includes, in addition to template matching, a whitening filter that flattens the power spectrum of the image noise, maximizing detectability against a spectrally inhomogeneous background.
evidence: Inference from the observation of low-frequency dominated noise and citation to matched filtering theory.

claim: Whitening restored detectability in simulated images with protein background.
source: We found that whitening, in fact, restored detectability: CCGs now showed strong and narrow peaks at the correct locations (Figure 4a).
evidence: Simulation results showing improved detection after applying whitening filter.

claim: Detectability with whitening was best for the PPM (SNR = 20.5) followed by 70 nm (SNR = 14.3) and 2000 nm (SNR = 7.7) underfocus.
source: Detectability was best (SNR = 20.5) for the PPM followed by 70 nm (SNR = 14.3) and 2000 nm (SNR = 7.7) underfocus.
evidence: Simulation results comparing SNR across imaging conditions with whitening.

claim: A major reason for compromised detectability in strongly defocused images is that the CTF does not suppress the low-frequency noise that dominates images with a high density of macromolecules.
source: These simulation results confirm that a major reason for compromised detectability in strongly defocused images is that there the CTF, unlike in close-to-focus images, does not suppress the low-frequency noise that dominates images with a high density of macromolecules.
evidence: Inference from simulation results comparing detectability across defocus values.

claim: A substantial part of the difference in SNRs between 70 and 2000 nm underfocus was due to illumination-coherence effects.
source: We also confirmed that a substantial part of the difference in SNRs between 70 and 2000 nm underfocus was due to illumination-coherence effects by repeating some of the simulations with completely coherent illumination.
evidence: Simulation results comparing partial and perfect coherence.

claim: Completely coherent illumination increased the SNR at 2000 nm by 42% (from 7.7 to 10.9).
source: This increased the SNR at 2000 nm by 42% (from 7.7 to 10.9), but only by 8% at 70 nm (from 14.3 to 15.4).
evidence: Simulation results comparing partial and perfect coherence at 2000 nm defocus.

claim: Completely coherent illumination increased the SNR at 70 nm by 8% (from 14.3 to 15.4).
source: This increased the SNR at 2000 nm by 42% (from 7.7 to 10.9), but only by 8% at 70 nm (from 14.3 to 15.4).
evidence: Simulation results comparing partial and perfect coherence at 70 nm defocus.

claim: The best SNR within the defocus range from 500 nm overfocus to 2000 nm underfocus was seen at 70 nm.
source: We also explored the SNR for a whole range of defocus values from 500 nm overfocus to 2000 nm underfocus (Figure 4b). Within this range, the best SNR was seen at 70 nm.
evidence: Simulation results scanning defocus values.

claim: Against a protein background, the SNR varied strongly with defocus near the Scherzer setting and then fell steadily with focus distance.
source: Against a protein background the SNR varied strongly with defocus near the Scherzer setting and then fell steadily with focus distance (Figure 4b), mitigated somewhat by whitening.
evidence: Simulation results showing SNR dependence on defocus with protein background.

claim: A background comprising randomly placed carbon atoms reduced protein detectability uniformly for all defocus settings.
source: In contrast, a background comprising randomly placed carbon atoms, which produced a spectrally flat noise distribution (data not shown), reduced protein detectability uniformly for all defocus settings (Figure 4b).
evidence: Simulation results with carbon atom background.

claim: For an isolated apoferritin molecule in vitreous ice, the average SNR for five particles increased until it reached a value of about 12 at a spatial frequency of 3 nm^-1 after which it essentially stayed constant.
source: For an isolated apoferritin molecule in vitreous ice, the average SNR for five of the particles in the experimental image increased until it reached a value of about 12 at a spatial frequency of 3 nm−1 after which it essentially stayed constant.
evidence: Experimental measurement of SNR vs. spatial frequency cutoff.

claim: In a simulation using the same parameters, the SNR closely followed the experimental curve up to a resolution of 2.4 nm^-1 beyond which it diverged upward to reach a value of 17.6 at 5.2 nm^-1.
source: In a simulation using the same parameters the SNR closely followed the experimental curve up to a resolution of 2.4 nm−1 beyond which it diverged upward to reach a value of 17.6 at 5.2 nm−1.
evidence: Simulation results matching experimental conditions.

claim: The difference between experimental and simulated SNR curves could be due to residual magnification or focus mismatch, uncorrected sample drift, or astigmatism in the experimental data.
source: The difference could be due to residual magnification or focus mismatch, uncorrected sample drift, or astigmatism in the experimental data (Figure 5a).
evidence: Speculation about sources of discrepancy between experiment and simulation.

claim: In simulations with protein background, the SNR for matched-filter detection reached maximum values of 14.7 and 8.3 at defocus settings of 70 and 2000 nm, respectively.
source: In simulations with protein background (Figure 5b), the SNR for matched-filter detection reached maximum values of 14.7 and 8.3 at defocus settings of 70 and 2000 nm, respectively.
evidence: Simulation results with protein background and whitening.

claim: The PPM outperformed both 70 nm and 2000 nm defocus settings throughout the spatial frequency range.
source: The PPM outperformed both settings throughout.
evidence: Simulation results comparing PPM to conventional defocus settings.

claim: Images close to focus performed best in precision-recall curves, largely independent of the SNR threshold.
source: Again and largely independent independent of the SNR threshold (which is varied to generate the PRC) images close to focus performed best, even when assuming perfect illumination coherence (Figure 5c).
evidence: Simulation results showing precision-recall curves for different imaging conditions.

claim: Rotavirus DLPs are 70 nm in diameter.
source: Rotavirus DLPs are 70 nm in diameter and have at their core a densely-packed double-stranded RNA genome (Estrozi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior structural characterization.

claim: Rotavirus DLPs have at their core a densely-packed double-stranded RNA genome.
source: Rotavirus DLPs are 70 nm in diameter and have at their core a densely-packed double-stranded RNA genome (Estrozi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior structural characterization.

claim: The genome is contained inside a protein shell assembled in perfect icosahedral symmetry from two protein types, VP2 and VP6.
source: The genome is contained inside a protein shell assembled in perfect icosahedral symmetry from two protein types, the inner capsid protein, VP2 (120 copies, approximately 90 kDa each), and the outer capsid protein, VP6 (780 copies, 45 kDa each), which together form 60 asymmetric subunits (ASUs, 720 kDa, Figure 6 inset).
evidence: Description of rotavirus DLP structure.

claim: VP2 is the inner capsid protein with 120 copies of approximately 90 kDa each.
source: The genome is contained inside a protein shell assembled in perfect icosahedral symmetry from two protein types, the inner capsid protein, VP2 (120 copies, approximately 90 kDa each), and the outer capsid protein, VP6 (780 copies, 45 kDa each), which together form 60 asymmetric subunits (ASUs, 720 kDa, Figure 6 inset).
evidence: Description of rotavirus DLP structure.

claim: VP6 is the outer capsid protein with 780 copies of 45 kDa each.
source: The genome is contained inside a protein shell assembled in perfect icosahedral symmetry from two protein types, the inner capsid protein, VP2 (120 copies, approximately 90 kDa each), and the outer capsid protein, VP6 (780 copies, 45 kDa each), which together form 60 asymmetric subunits (ASUs, 720 kDa, Figure 6 inset).
evidence: Description of rotavirus DLP structure.

claim: VP2 and VP6 together form 60 asymmetric subunits (ASUs) of 720 kDa.
source: The genome is contained inside a protein shell assembled in perfect icosahedral symmetry from two protein types, the inner capsid protein, VP2 (120 copies, approximately 90 kDa each), and the outer capsid protein, VP6 (780 copies, 45 kDa each), which together form 60 asymmetric subunits (ASUs, 720 kDa, Figure 6 inset).
evidence: Description of rotavirus DLP structure.

claim: Each DLP contains at least two enzymatic proteins, VP1 (at least 11 copies, 115 kDa each) and VP3 (at least 11 copies, 90–100 kDa each).
source: In addition to these structural proteins, each DLP contains at least two enzymatic proteins, VP1 (at least 11 copies, 115 kDa each) and VP3 (at least 11 copies, 90–100 kDa each), which together are responsible for synthesizing and capping single-stranded RNA molecules before they are extruded into the infected host cell (Ogden et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on rotavirus structure and function.

claim: VP1 and VP3 together are responsible for synthesizing and capping single-stranded RNA molecules before they are extruded into the infected host cell.
source: In addition to these structural proteins, each DLP contains at least two enzymatic proteins, VP1 (at least 11 copies, 115 kDa each) and VP3 (at least 11 copies, 90–100 kDa each), which together are responsible for synthesizing and capping single-stranded RNA molecules before they are extruded into the infected host cell (Ogden et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on rotavirus function.

claim: The projected density of biological macromolecules in the DLP is around 20 kDa nm^-2 across most of the particle.
source: The projected density of biological macromolecules in the DLP is around 20 kDa nm−2 across most of the particle, which is similar to the density (20–30 kDa nm−2) expected for a 100 nm-thick section of tissue (Ellis, 2001).
evidence: Calculation based on DLP structure and comparison to tissue density from citation.

claim: The projected density of biological macromolecules in the DLP is similar to the density (20–30 kDa nm^-2) expected for a 100 nm-thick section of tissue.
source: The projected density of biological macromolecules in the DLP is around 20 kDa nm−2 across most of the particle, which is similar to the density (20–30 kDa nm−2) expected for a 100 nm-thick section of tissue (Ellis, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on cellular macromolecular density.

claim: Most (93.3% for 1400–1600 nm defocus and 99.7% for 270–310 nm defocus) of the CCG values above the detection threshold occurred within 0.5 nm and five degrees of the expected locations and orientations.
source: When searching these images for ASUs, using the full set of Hopf rotations and a whitening filter, we found that most (93.3% for 1400–1600 nm defocus and 99.7% for 270–310 nm defocus) of the CCG values above the detection threshold occurred within 0.5 nm and five degrees of the expected locations and orientations (Figure 6b).
evidence: Experimental results from searching DLP images for ASUs.

claim: The superiority of images taken close to focus persists along most of the precision-recall curve.
source: The superiority of images taken close to focus, a central prediction of our simulations, persists along most of the precision-recall curve (Figure 6c).
evidence: Experimental precision-recall curves for DLP images at different defocus values.

claim: The number of pixels where the noise alone generates CCG values above a given threshold increases with the number of independent LOCs searched.
source: The number of pixels where the noise alone generates CCG values above a given threshold increases with the number of independent LOCs searched while the threshold needed to obtain a certain detection rate decreases as the molecular weight of the target falls (Figure 2b).
evidence: Based on statistical properties of noise and the number of independent tests.

claim: The threshold needed to obtain a certain detection rate decreases as the molecular weight of the target falls.
source: The number of pixels where the noise alone generates CCG values above a given threshold increases with the number of independent LOCs searched while the threshold needed to obtain a certain detection rate decreases as the molecular weight of the target falls (Figure 2b).
evidence: Based on the observed square-root dependence of SNR on molecular weight.

claim: For proteins below a certain size, a meaningful search of the entire LOC space is no longer possible.
source: This means that for proteins below a certain size a meaningful search of the entire LOC space is no longer possible, which puts many proteins out of reach.
evidence: Inference from the relationship between molecular weight, SNR, and false alarm rate.

claim: The size limit for unconstrained detection is around 150 kDa for isolated targets.
source: Our data (Figure 2b) suggest that the size limit is around 150 kDa for isolated targets, and should be about twice that with protein background, which reduces the SNR by about 30% (Figure 4b).
evidence: Inference from experimental data on molecular weight dependence of SNR.

claim: The size limit for unconstrained detection should be about twice 150 kDa (i.e., 300 kDa) with protein background.
source: Our data (Figure 2b) suggest that the size limit is around 150 kDa for isolated targets, and should be about twice that with protein background, which reduces the SNR by about 30% (Figure 4b).
evidence: Inference from the observed 30% reduction in SNR with protein background.

claim: Prior information about the location or orientation of the target reduces the total number of false alarms and should allow the detection of much smaller targets.
source: While prior information about the location or orientation of the target does not reduce the chance that for a particular LOC the detection threshold is breached by the noise, it does reduce the total number of false alarms because fewer LOCs need to be searched and thus should allow the detection of much smaller targets.
evidence: Logical inference from the relationship between search space size and false alarm rate.

claim: VP1 is an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that binds to the inner surface of the DLP capsid.
source: We explored this idea by performing a constrained search for VP1, an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that binds to the inner surface of the DLP capsid (Estrozi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: Given knowledge of all ASU LOCs, the number of LOCs that need to be searched for VP1 is reduced from about 10^12 to below 10^3.
source: Given that we know the LOCs of all ASUs, the number of LOCs that need to be searched is reduced from about 1012 to below 103.
evidence: Calculation based on the constraint to ASU locations.

claim: Using a threshold of 2.03, an average of 9.63 VP1s per DLP were found.
source: Using a threshold of 2.03, which yielded, on average, 0.059 false alarms per ASU LOC for a set of control templates (Materials and methods), we found 9.63 VP1s per DLP.
evidence: Experimental results from constrained search for VP1.

claim: Assuming 11 bound VP1s per DLP, about 2.9 of the detected VP1s should be false alarms leaving 6.73 true positives, a recall of 71.2%.
source: Assuming 11 bound VP1s per DLP, about 2.9 (0.059 × (60-11)) of those should be false alarms leaving 6.73 true positives, a recall of 71.2%.
evidence: Calculation based on false alarm rate and assumed number of VP1s.

claim: The prevalence of vertices that contained one detected VP1 was substantially larger than the binomially distributed prevalence expected for independent binding.
source: The prevalence of vertices that contained one detected VP1 was substantially larger (and those with zero, two, or three substantially smaller) than the binomially distributed prevalence one would expect for independent binding and what one gets with the binding sites randomly shuffled within each DLP (Figure 6d).
evidence: Statistical analysis of VP1 detection distribution across vertices.

claim: The VP1 detection distribution is consistent with the assumption that steric hindrances prevent the binding of more than one VP1 per vertex.
source: This is consistent with the assumption that steric hindrances prevent the binding of more than one VP1 per vertex (Estrozi et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference from detection distribution and citation to prior structural work.

claim: The SNR of 2.28 for VP1 detection is smaller than the value of 2.98 expected by extrapolation from ASU detection.
source: The SNR of 2.28, estimated from CCG histograms (Materials and methods), is smaller than the value of 2.98 that one gets by extrapolation from 7.45, the mean peak value seen when searching for ASUs, using the square-root dependence of the SNR on the molecular mass (Figure 2b).
evidence: Comparison of observed and expected SNR values.

claim: The lower than expected SNR for VP1 is likely due to differences between the X-ray-derived and the in situ structure of VP1.
source: This is likely due to differences between the X-ray-derived and the in situ structure of VP1 (see below).
evidence: Inference from the observed structural differences in the reconstruction.

claim: The resulting VP1 potential distribution includes a well-resolved VP1 molecule attached to one of the five possible binding sites near an ssRNA exit portal.
source: The resulting potential distribution includes a well-resolved VP1 molecule attached to one of the five possible binding sites near an ssRNA exit portal (Figure 6e).
evidence: Reconstruction from detection-triggered averaging.

claim: The differences between the reconstructed VP1 structure and the structure used to generate the templates are most numerous near the contact to the capsid.
source: Unlike detection, reconstruction can be affected by template bias, but the differences between our VP1 structure and the structure used to generate the templates, which are most numerous near the contact to the capsid (Figure 6e, Supplementary file 1) and include an α-helix in close contact with both the polymerase and the exit portal (Figure 6e, red arrow), cannot due to template bias (Henderson, 2013) as they are not part of the template.
evidence: Analysis of difference map between reconstruction and template.

claim: The α-helix in close contact with both the polymerase and the exit portal cannot be due to template bias as it is not part of the template.
source: Unlike detection, reconstruction can be affected by template bias, but the differences between our VP1 structure and the structure used to generate the templates, which are most numerous near the contact to the capsid (Figure 6e, Supplementary file 1) and include an α-helix in close contact with both the polymerase and the exit portal (Figure 6e, red arrow), cannot due to template bias (Henderson, 2013) as they are not part of the template.
evidence: Logical argument that features not in template cannot be due to template bias, supported by citation.

claim: The α-helix could well be part of the RNA-capping enzyme VP3.
source: This helix could well be part of the RNA-capping enzyme VP3, whose structure (Brandmann and Jinek, 2015; Ogden et al., 2015) contains a helix of appropriate length and is proposed to reside near VP1 (Gridley and Patton, 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on VP3 structure and proposed location, supported by citations.

claim: The reconstruction shows structural features in the nucleic acid regions of the density map near VP1 that were not seen in icosahedrally symmetric reconstructions.
source: In addition to proteins, the reconstruction also shows structural features in the nucleic acid regions of the density map near VP1 that were not seen in icosahedrally symmetric reconstructions (Estrozi et al., 2013) (Figure 6e).
evidence: Comparison of current reconstruction to prior icosahedrally averaged reconstruction.

claim: High-resolution template matching can detect proteins of known structure in single cryo-EM images with high selectivity.
source: We have shown that high-resolution template matching can detect—with high selectivity—proteins of known structure in single cryo-EM images and determine—with high precision—their orientation and projected location.
evidence: Summary of experimental results demonstrating detection capability.

claim: High-resolution template matching can determine the orientation and projected location of proteins with high precision.
source: We have shown that high-resolution template matching can detect—with high selectivity—proteins of known structure in single cryo-EM images and determine—with high precision—their orientation and projected location.
evidence: Summary of experimental results demonstrating precision of orientation and location determination.

claim: When combined with whitening, the approach can detect moderately sized proteins even when they are surrounded by a high density of other proteins.
source: When combined with whitening this approach can detect moderately sized proteins even when they are surrounded by a high density of other proteins, as is the case when trying to detect components of individual macromolecular assemblies and determine their spatial arrangement.
evidence: Summary of simulation and experimental results with protein background.

claim: Operating close to focus helps in the detection of target proteins by suppressing low spatial-frequencies caused by the presence of other proteins.
source: We found that operating close to focus helps in the detection of target proteins first by suppressing low spatial-frequencies (which are critical when picking particles for single-particle averaging) caused by the presence of other proteins and, second, by preserving high frequency information crucial for sensitivity and selectivity.
evidence: Summary of simulation results showing improved detection at close-to-focus.

claim: Operating close to focus helps in the detection of target proteins by preserving high frequency information crucial for sensitivity and selectivity.
source: We found that operating close to focus helps in the detection of target proteins first by suppressing low spatial-frequencies (which are critical when picking particles for single-particle averaging) caused by the presence of other proteins and, second, by preserving high frequency information crucial for sensitivity and selectivity.
evidence: Summary of simulation results showing improved detection at close-to-focus.

claim: The irreversible loss of high-frequency information due to partial-coherence effects becomes more severe at larger defocus.
source: While the suppression of low frequencies can also be achieved by filtering the acquired images, the irreversible loss of high-frequency information that occurs due to partial-coherence effects becomes more severe at larger defocus and was responsible for the degraded detection sensitivity seen in simulated large-defocus images.
evidence: Simulation results comparing coherent and partially coherent illumination at different defocus values.

claim: The inclusion of higher spatial frequencies in both templates and in the image improves the detection sensitivity.
source: While the inclusion of higher spatial frequencies in both templates and in the image improves the detection sensitivity (Figure 5b), it also exacerbates the differences between a particular reference structure (usually determined in a non-native context such as a crystal) and its conformation in situ (Figure 6e, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Simulation results showing SNR increase with spatial frequency and observation of structural differences.

claim: The inclusion of higher spatial frequencies exacerbates the differences between a reference structure and its conformation in situ.
source: While the inclusion of higher spatial frequencies in both templates and in the image improves the detection sensitivity (Figure 5b), it also exacerbates the differences between a particular reference structure (usually determined in a non-native context such as a crystal) and its conformation in situ (Figure 6e, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Observation of structural differences between template and reconstruction.

claim: Searches may need to include template sets for a whole range of possible conformations.
source: Searches may, therefore, need to include template sets for a whole range of possible conformations.
evidence: Inference from the observation of structural differences between reference and in situ structures.

claim: Magnification and focus will need to be estimated more precisely.
source: Finally, magnification and focus will need to be estimated more precisely and the orientation, in particular, sampled more densely.
evidence: Inference from sensitivity analysis showing SNR dependence on these parameters.

claim: Orientation will need to be sampled more densely.
source: Finally, magnification and focus will need to be estimated more precisely and the orientation, in particular, sampled more densely.
evidence: Inference from sensitivity analysis showing SNR dependence on orientation.

claim: Whether detection of proteins above 300 kDa is possible in 100 nm-thick slices of vitrified biological material should be testable with modern cryo-sectioning techniques.
source: Whether detection of proteins above 300 kDa is possible in 100 nm-thick slices of vitrified biological material should be testable with the help of modern cryo-sectioning techniques (Al-Amoudi et al., 2007).
evidence: Speculation about future experiments, supported by citation to cryo-sectioning methods.

claim: At 300 keV and an exposure of 1000 electrons/nm^2, a single apoferritin molecule scatters about 1436 electrons elastically.
source: At 300 keV and an exposure of 1000 electrons/nm2, a single apoferritin molecule scatters about 1436 (Materials and methods) electrons elastically, of which about 20% are available at a resolution of 0.4 nm.
evidence: Calculation based on atomic scattering cross-sections.

claim: About 20% of the elastically scattered electrons from apoferritin are available at a resolution of 0.4 nm.
source: At 300 keV and an exposure of 1000 electrons/nm2, a single apoferritin molecule scatters about 1436 (Materials and methods) electrons elastically, of which about 20% are available at a resolution of 0.4 nm.
evidence: Calculation based on scattering angles.

claim: Taking into account that due to the oscillation in the CTF only half of the high-frequency electrons are usable, the expected SNR is approximately 12.
source: Taking into account that due to the oscillation in the CTF only half of those are usable we expect a SNR of ≈12 ((1436 × 0.2 × 0.5)0.5), which is close to what is seen (Figure 1).
evidence: Calculation based on scattered electron count and comparison to experimental SNR.

claim: If all scattered electrons could be used, the SNR would increase to almost 38.
source: If all scattered electrons could be used, the SNR would increase to almost 38.
evidence: Calculation based on total scattered electron count.

claim: The minimal molecular weight for detection, assuming perfect electron-optical resolution, a B-factor of 0, no background, and a SNR of about seven, would be around 16 kDa.
source: The minimal molecular weight—assuming perfect electron-optical resolution, a B-factor of 0, no background, and a SNR of about seven needed for detection—would then be around 16 kDa.
evidence: Calculation based on ideal conditions and square-root dependence of SNR on molecular weight.

claim: Detection of the rotavirus RNA polymerase and the mapping of the occupied binding sites inside the virus capsid illustrates how one can analyze partially stochastic protein assemblies.
source: Detection of the rotavirus RNA polymerase and the mapping of the occupied binding sites inside the virus capsid (Figure 6d–e) illustrates how one can analyze partially stochastic protein assemblies, in which a ligand protein (here, VP1) binds at only some of the available binding sites on a molecular host (the virus capsid).
evidence: Summary of VP1 detection results and their implications.

claim: If the steric constraints of the interaction are known, even ligands below the unconstrained detection limit should be detectable.
source: If the steric constraints of the interaction are known (Figure 6d–e), even ligands below the unconstrained detection limit should be detectable.
evidence: Inference from successful detection of VP1 using constrained search.

claim: Apoferritin samples were prepared to a final protein concentration of 0.25 mg/mL in PBS.
source: Apoferritin samples were prepared to a final protein concentration of 0.25 mg/mL in PBS from horse-spleen apoferritin (#A3660, lot #SLBF8335V, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) and contained 15 nm gold particles (#1115, Nanoprobes, Yaphank, NY).
evidence: Description of experimental sample preparation.

claim: Electron cryo-microscopy was performed on a TEM operated at 300 kV.
source: Electron cryo-microscopy was performed on a transmission electron microscope (TEM) operated at 300 kV (Titan Krios, FEI, Hillsboro, OR) in parallel illumination mode.
evidence: Description of experimental imaging conditions.

claim: Image data were recorded as movies with an exposure time of 25 msec per frame at a nominal magnification of 59,000 in counting mode.
source: Image data were recorded as movies with an exposure time of 25 msec per frame at a nominal magnification of 59,000 in counting mode, which resulted in a sample-referred pixel pitch of 0.0482 nm.
evidence: Description of experimental data acquisition parameters.

claim: The sample-referred pixel pitch was 0.0482 nm.
source: Image data were recorded as movies with an exposure time of 25 msec per frame at a nominal magnification of 59,000 in counting mode, which resulted in a sample-referred pixel pitch of 0.0482 nm.
evidence: Calculated from magnification and detector pixel size.
